highlights.text: Units put together, or the putting together of units; al-Rāghib says the two definitions are the same.
highlights.note: al-Raghib's definition of al-'adad, the root's base sense

highlights.text: Joining numbers one to another.
A thing that is "counted and enumerated" (maʿdūd) is few
"We have not made their number" (Q 74:31) means their count.
"I made this ready for you" means "I placed it so that you can count on it and take it as you need it."
Al-Rāghib defines it as the days after which it becomes lawful for her to marry.
highlights.note: a legal definition of a woman's 'idda

highlights.text: Some jurists instead count the day of sacrifice and the two days after it as the "counted days".
FIRST ROOT — evenness, equality, straightness
highlights.note: the first of Ibn Faris's two roots

highlights.text: SECOND ROOT — crookedness/deviation
ʿadl = one who is approved and straight in conduct; upright.
ʿadl = judging by equity, deciding evenly.
the mushrik who yaʿdilu bi-rabbihi — treating another as equal to his Lord.
highlights.note: the entry's reading of the Qur'an's ya'dilun bi-rabbihim

highlights.text: A verse of Zuhayr uses ʿadl of trusted arbiters who are "accepted, and just."
has no single underlying sense that unifies its uses
highlights.note: Ibn Faris: no one sense unites the root

highlights.text: the well-known legume — lentils — is called "ʿadas."
"When I load my gear upon ʿadas," where "ʿadas" stands for the female mule herself
one sound root whose whole family turns on a single idea: going beyond something, overstepping the limit at which one ought to stop
Going past one's proper bounds.
The ʿādī is one who assaults people wrongfully (ẓulman wa-ʿudwānan).
Derived from the same root; the one form serves singular, dual, and plural.
Cited with Qurʾān 26:77 (Abraham: "they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the Worlds")
Cited with Zuhayr, where a distraction (ʿadāʾ) kept the poet from his beloved.
felling one after the other (cited with Imruʾ al-Qays)
cited with the ḥadīth "No ʿadwā, and nothing transmits [disease] to anything."
refraining from what is foul, and the scantness of something
al-ʿiffa is refraining from what is not fitting.
Al-ʿufra names a color: dust-gray shading into red. From this, plain earth/soil itself is called al-ʿafar.
highlights.note: sense 1, the dust-red sense the entry traces others back to

highlights.text: A strong, bold, or cunningly wicked man is "ʿifr" — hence "shayṭānun ʿifriyatun / ʿifrītun" (a devilish, formidable one)
Cited in verse by al-Aʿshā, both for the tree/fire-sticks and possibly as the origin of the woman's name "ʿAfāra"
illustrated by a verse of Labīd about an abandoned/intermittently-fed fawn
A ḥadīth about Hilāl b. Umayya using "ʿaffarnā" is connected to palm-pollination (al-ʿafār).
a ḥadīth condemning God's dislike of such a person
TWO base ideas: (1) leaving/abandoning a thing (tark), and (2) seeking a thing (ṭalab).
al-ʿafw — pardon. God's ʿafw toward His creation is His leaving them unpunished, as a bounty.
Al-Khalīl: whoever deserves punishment and you leave him, you have "ʿafawta ʿanhu" (pardoned him).
Qurʾānic shāhid: {ḥattā ʿafaw} (al-Aʿrāf 95), glossed "until they grew and multiplied,"
Shāhid: Labīd's "The abodes are effaced… left desolate (taʾabbada)."
as in the Prophet's "I have pardoned you as to the ṣadaqa of horses," meaning "I have left off imposing it,"
Hadith shāhid: reviving dead land, "what the ʿāfiya eat of it is a ṣadaqa."
a single core idea, which he credits to al-Khalīl: guarding or keeping something, and renewing one's contact with it.
عَهِدَ (ʿahida) means to enjoin or charge, akin to a bequest (waṣiyya)
الْعَهْد is a binding pledge or solemn compact (mawthiq); plural ʿuhūd.
عَهِيدُك is one who mutually covenants with you
"did I not set before you, and make binding on you to keep, the matter I enjoined."
with a verse of al-Ṭirimmāḥ on a man who "does not tend to" what God made binding on him
highlights.note: al-Tirimmah, Umayyad; the entry names no earlier poet

highlights.text: أهل العهد / المُعَاهَدُون are those bound under covenant regarding the jizya due from them
softness, ease, and scantiness of sustenance/substance in a thing.
Al-ihn - dyed wool: Ibn Faris judges it plausible that this word too belongs to the same root-family
A saying distinguishes a cash sale from a credit sale: "did you sell ahin [cash-in-hand] or on credit?"
a line of al-Nabigha where a camel is urged on because "short of the watering-place there is no ahin to hold you back."
a hadith in which the Prophet tells a companion to bring him palm-fronds but avoid the awahin, "because they are moist,"
one about deeming something great/being conceited, the other a part of an animal's body.
ʿajiba yaʿjabu ʿajaban ("to marvel")
aʿjabanī hādhā l-shayʾ ("this thing pleased me")
"and one astonished at the composure he sees in us — yet had war shoved him, he would not have stirred."
Leanness / emaciation (al-ʿajaf)
Restraint of the self, endurance toward or away from something
The word means the loss of fatness, thinness.
Adjective forms: masculine aʿjaf, feminine ʿajfāʾ, plural (for both sexes) ʿijāf.
He quotes a verse by Ibn Abī ʿĀʾidh describing arrows as ʿijāf al-niṣāl, "lean/slender of arrowhead."
two distinct sound roots: (1) haste/speed, and (2) a particular animal (the calf).
istaʿjala someone = urged him on; ʿajila someone = outstripped/got ahead of him.
ʿājil = the opposite of ājil (the deferred). Hence this world = al-ʿājila (the hastening/present)
al-ʿijl = the young of the cow
proverb: "the traveller's quick provision is dates and sawīq (parched-barley meal)."
ʿujma is the opposite of clear expression (ibāna), and iʿjām is leaving something obscure or indistinct.
ʿAjam is the counterpart of ʿArab, and ʿajamī is the adjective of relation to them.
But aʿjam denotes anyone whose speech is indistinct, Arab or not
an Arab saying, "I went out from lands that speak," as a figure for lands that are inhabited and cultivated.
"the daytime prayer is ʿajmāʾ," meaning the recitation in it is not said aloud; and "the wound caused by a beast carries no compensation."
highlights.note: two sayings: one on the prayer, one a legal maxim

highlights.text: two sound roots: (1) weakness/inability, and (2) the hind-part or rear of a thing.
أَعْجَزَنِي فلان = "he eluded me," i.e. I could not pursue and overtake him.
عَجُوز ("old woman"), plural عَجَائِز
عَجُز = the back or rear of a thing, plural أَعْجَاز
Proverb: "a man inevitably grows incapable."
Proverb: "do not busy yourselves with the tail-ends of matters whose fronts have already passed."
facing or turning toward something (muqābala), and holding back or confining (ḥabs).
highlights.note: Ibn Faris's one root, two linked ideas

highlights.text: the one who keeps himself to a place or thing.
al-maʿkūf means al-maḥbūs, the one detained or prevented.
"We left the horses staying over him, their reins hung on their necks, standing [motionless]."
a mark or trace on a thing by which it is told apart from others
highlights.note: Ibn Faris reduces every sense to this

highlights.text: ʿilm — knowledge, the opposite of ignorance (jahl).
taʿallama — to learn, i.e. to acquire knowledge (ʿilm) of a thing
al-ʿālamūn — the "worlds," i.e. the kinds of creation
the idiom taʿallam anna… used to mean "know that…" (equivalent to iʿlam), attested in a line of Qays ibn Zuhayr.
took it to refer to the descent of Jesus, by which the Hour's nearness is known.
a thing's being made manifest, being pointed to, and becoming apparent
أَعْلَنْتُهُ (aʿlantuhu) — "I made it public, disclosed it."
a single underlying idea: **that a thing be hung on, or fastened to, something above it**
ʿaliqa bi- ("to cling to, stick fast to")
al-ʿalaq is congealed blood; a single piece is ʿalaqa. Ibn Fāris says the analogy holds because such blood clings.
Ibn Fāris glosses: the woman who is neither husbandless nor possessed of a husband, as though her affair were unsettled.
Muhalhil: "…and a stubborn adversary, one of miʿlāq."
Al-Aʿshā: "I was made to love her by chance, and she was attached to another man, and he to yet another woman."
in the ḥadīth of the martyrs the birds "browse (taʿluq) in the Garden."
He pairs it with the ḥadīth of Umm Zarʿ: "If I speak I am divorced; if I keep silent I am left suspended."
a single root meaning loftiness and elevation, from which nothing departs.
تَعَالَى النَّهَارُ = "the day climbed high."
al-ʿalāʾ specifically means elevation of rank, while al-ʿuluww can mean greatness and overbearing tyranny
عَلَا الْمَلِكُ فِي الْأَرْضِ ("the king exalted himself arrogantly in the land"), as in Q 28:4 of Pharaoh
تَعَالَ ("come!"). From ʿuluww — originally "ascend to me"
Poetic evidence (Aws, Umayya b. Abī al-Ṣalt read by al-Aṣmaʿī): al-ʿālī = a grave, crushing affliction
highlights.note: Aws and Umayya b. Abi al-Salt, pre-Islamic

highlights.text: al-ʿalyāʾ = a mountain-top or high ground (Zuhayr)
Al-Farrāʾ: "elevation upon elevation without limit."
a single idea: **straightness in a thing — either standing upright or extending lengthwise — and the same straightness in opinion and in intending something.**
عَمَدْتُ فلاناً, "I made for him," i.e. aimed at him on purpose.
Hence الْعَمْد, the opposite of خطأ (accident/error) in killing and in other matters
Al-Khalīl: ʿamd is to hold a thing up with a عِمَاد that supports it and on which it rests.
On {فِي عَمَدٍ مُمَدَّدَةٍ} (104:9): "in something like tents of stretched-out fire"
"Suʿād has departed, and the eye's sleep is sleeplessness / and the heart is downcast, burning, propped up."
highlights.note: al-Akhtal, Umayyad; the entry names no earlier poet

highlights.text: al-Mubarrad's sense — رجلٌ مُعْمَدٌ means "tall," and الْعِمَاد means tallness/height — so "possessed of loftiness."
He supports this with the ḥadīth phrase "he is lofty of column, long of sword-belt."
bewilderment and a poor ability to find one's way.
a man is described this way when he casts about back and forth, not knowing which direction to take.
one general sense: it covers every act or deed that is performed.
عَمِلَ means "to work, to act"; the agent is عامِل ("worker, doer")
illustrated by a line of verse: the noble man labours with his own hands when he has no one else to lean on.
one sound root which, in his account, indicates tallness, abundance and height.
citing Labīd's tall, lush palms (ʿamm) with vines between them.
Labīd speaks of guests' bowls filled with pure milk that is muʿammam, "turbaned".
one core, physical sense — depth/farness downward
highlights.note: Ibn Faris / Ibn al-A'rabi: the core sense

highlights.text: Said of a road: al-ʿumq means "distance, farness" (al-buʿd).
the saying mā abʿada ʿamāqata hādhihi r-rakiyyah, "how deep this well is!"
an eloquent Arab quoted by Ibn al-Aʿrābī said, "I saw a khalīqah [a freshly-dug well], and never saw one deeper."
highlights.note: a speaker of the Arabs, via Ibn al-A'rabi

highlights.text: (1) remaining and the extension of time, and (2) something that rises high
al-ʿumr, also al-ʿamr: life. The oath laʿamruka ("by your life") swears by a person's life.
ʿammarahum Allāh taʿmīran: God gave them long life.
ʿimārat al-arḍ, inhabiting and cultivating the land
In Ibn Aḥmar's line "its riders raise their voices at al-Farqad, as the riding muʿtamir raises his voice"
